title: God's Love and Anxiety
speaker: Mr. Steve Thomas
series: Calm in the Character of God
summary: This lesson explores God's love as the antidote to anxiety by examining multiple dimensions of God's love: holy, forgiving, satisfying, faithful, fatherly, everlasting, displayed in Christ, and transforming. Through Scripture and personal reflection, the speaker emphasizes that meditating on God's character—particularly His love—is the key to overcoming sinful worry and anxiety.

outline.title: Review of the Anxiety Series and Biblical Framework
subpoints: Anxiety is reframed as a spiritual issue, not merely a brain-body problem
The difference between prudent care/planning and sinful anxiety: worry becomes sinful when unproductive and not centered on God
God's character attributes provide comfort only to believers; unbelievers have reason to be anxious without Christ
Christ reshapes hearts through trials, conforming believers to His image

outline.title: God's Love is Holy
subpoints: God is perfectly holy and cannot tolerate evil; this is the foundation for understanding His love
Our sin creates an insurmountable obstacle between us and God's holiness
Christ's righteousness imputed to us resolves the conflict between God's holiness and His love through substitutionary atonement
We cannot understand God's love apart from understanding His holiness

outline.title: God's Love is Forgiving
subpoints: All of our sins—without exception—are forgiven through Christ's sacrifice
Unconfessed sin creates anxiety and discord with God; we must confess all sin, not hold back 'pet sins'
Confessing sin restores fellowship and peace with God, replacing anxiety with joy
God's forgiveness is the source of peace with the Creator and Judge of the universe

outline.title: God's Love is Satisfying
subpoints: God's love must be tasted and experienced, not merely intellectually affirmed
Meditate on concrete ways God has demonstrated His love in your life, filling your mind with truth about His love
As we meditate on God's satisfying love, anxiety loses space in our minds
God's loving-kindness is better than life itself

outline.title: God's Love is Faithful and Everlasting
subpoints: God never changes, never forgets, and never deserts His people
Even when family and friends betray us, our heavenly Father remains faithful
God's mercies are new every morning; His love endures forever
Nothing can separate us from the love of God

outline.title: God's Love is Fatherly
subpoints: God remembers our weaknesses and has compassion on us as a father does his children
God exercises perfect, tender fatherly love that surpasses earthly fathers
Through adoption, God makes us His children; His love depends on Christ's merit, not ours
When we worry, we reject God's fatherly love and doubt His promises

outline.title: God's Love is Displayed in Christ and is Transforming
subpoints: God so loved the world that He sent His only begotten Son to die for us—the ultimate proof of His love
If God did not withhold His own Son, how can we doubt His love in daily trials?
God's transforming love means all things work together for good for those called according to His purpose
Trials and suffering are blessings that conform us to the image of Christ, not signs of God's absence
We can abide in Christ's love even in persecution; full joy comes through abiding in His love

transcript:
## Introduction and Series Context

Okay, so this morning we're going to continue our study through anxiety and how we deal with anxiety biblically. This morning we're going to be talking about considering God's love and how that impacts our anxiety and our worry.

Bear with me. I'm still getting over a cold, so I've got a cough drop and some tea. If you want to grab a Bible and turn to Matthew chapter 6, we're going to be considering that passage. Before we read that passage, I want to do a little bit of review. I think it's important that we review where we've been in this study because of the revolutionary—not revolutionary, but revolutionary in today's culture—way that we're looking at anxiety.

I definitely see some new faces here who weren't here at the beginning of the series, so I want to go over why we're considering anxiety the way that we are. I'm not going to present the entire thesis of the study, because that's been several lessons. But all of the lessons that build the basis for what I'm going to say are on our Spotify, Apple Podcast, and elsewhere. Several lessons build out what I'm about to say.

## Review: The World's View vs. Scripture's View

As we've considered anxiety, we've considered it through the lens of what the world says—as a brain-body issue. We've considered anxiety through what Scripture says—as a spiritual issue—and I want to remind us of why we're doing this study at all.

The world would have us consider anxiety as a brain-body issue: something that we can medicate, something that we can get over through counseling. It is a truly medical issue. But without dismissing the real pain and suffering that are involved in anxiety, we've also considered what Scripture has to say about this truly dominant issue in our culture today.

Scripture clearly places anxiety in the spiritual realm, not just in the physical realm. This is based on, among other things, the command in Matthew 6 not to be anxious, a study of the inner man and outer man (the inner man being spiritual, the outer man being physical) in 2 Corinthians, and commands to take every thought captive. We've considered that we have a high priest—Jesus—who is tempted in every way just like we are, yet without sin.

## The Difference Between Prudent Care and Sinful Worry

We've also considered the difference between prudent planning and care, and sinful worry and anxiety. Can anybody remind me: What did we say is the difference between sinful anxiety and prudent care and concern planning? Anybody remember?

When we're not considering God, when we're spinning out and not carefully planning, when we're not being productive in that planning—that's when we've crossed from care and planning into worry. Worry is when it's not productive. It's not "here are concrete steps that I can take right now to fix this," but rather "I'm going to fixate on this problem" rather than fixating on God.

Again, without dismissing some of the very real suffering that we often respond to with anxiety, we have considered anxiety not as something that happens to us, but rather as a way that we respond to the circumstances that God has placed us in.

## God's Character as the Antidote to Anxiety

As we've reframed the way that we look at anxiety, we've also considered what Scripture says about anxiety and how we can righteously combat this sin in our life. And that's by meditating on the character of God. That's exactly where Jesus points us in Matthew 6. When we're told to be anxious for nothing, but rather we need to consider how the Father sustains the lilies. That's led into the last several weeks as we've considered different aspects of God's character:

- His fatherhood—the way that He relates to Christians
- His aseity—His self-existence outside of anything else
- His omniscience—His complete, unchanging, everlasting, perfect knowledge of all things, including our own hearts
- His sovereignty—His complete control over all things, including the things that we're responding to with anxiety

And perhaps most importantly, we've considered that as great of a comfort as all of these truths are about God in our struggle against anxiety, all of these truths are comfort only to the believer.

## A Word to Unbelievers

I want to take a second to dwell on that. These comforts of God's character absolutely should help the believer defeat anxiety in their life. But they're not a promise of hope to the unbeliever.

I hope through our lesson today, as we consider the love of God, that you're able to see a clear presentation of the gospel if you are not a believer, if you do not have Jesus as your Lord and Savior. I believe that you will see a clear presentation of the gospel. But I want to be clear: the unbeliever does have every reason to be anxious.

The very God who works all things for good for His people—for those who are called according to His purpose—is not working all things for good if you are not called according to His purpose. He doesn't extend that same promise to those who rebel against Him.

For the believer, God promises a hard life that is full of trials. But it is a hard life with a point: we're being conformed to the image of Christ. So consider as we look at the love of God—consider Christ as He's presented, consider the forgiveness that He offers, and the meaning that gives to the suffering that we have. We're going to return to this later at the end of the lesson.

But I want you to examine your own hearts. Christianity is not a cure-all for all of life's problems. Let me rephrase that: trusting in Christ is a cure-all for all of life's problems. But it's not in the way that we might expect. Christ reshapes our hearts, and while we're led through trials, those trials ultimately conform us to the image of Christ. So we can ultimately recognize those trials as the greatest good that could have possibly happened to us.

## Personal Testimony and Vulnerability

Every speaker in this series has mentioned the next point. As we continue in review, it bears repeating. As you've heard from each of the men that have taught, you've heard sometimes deeply personal struggles with anxiety. They've shared the ways in which they themselves have grappled with anxiety, the ways in which God's word and God's character have been an encouragement to them.

I think this bears drawing out just a little. To be clear, I don't think that's something that any of us planned. We didn't sit down and talk about "Hey, this would be something that's helpful." I can't speak for every one of the teachers, but as I consider this lesson in this series, it's laid heavy with me that I don't want to approach this topic from the perspective of throwing stones from a glass house. I imagine that's on everybody else's mind too.

So when we strongly call anxiety a sin—which it is—my fear is that for the saint that's struggling with anxiety, what you hear is "Stop sinning. How could you be anxious? Just knock it off." With anxiety, that feels impossible. And through our own strength, it is impossible. That's the point of this series. We fight anxiety not just by stopping being anxious, but by filling our minds with the character of God.

You've heard earlier in the series through an oblique reference about a struggle with anxiety and PTSD that my family went through a few years ago, lasting for a while. The whole story isn't needed here today—it would take more time than I have to tell that whole story. But what helped was not the secular counseling with its coping strategies and copays. What helped was examining the issue through the lens of Scripture: examining the suffering that I was going through, the sinful responses that I had, the way that Christ was tempted in every way just like I was, and yet without sin, through suffering much greater.

I'm happy to talk with anybody about that, not in this setting—like I said, that story would take much too long to tell here, and it's not the point. But leaning on a Savior that knows my every weakness, my every sin, my every temptation, and yet gave Himself up as a sacrifice for me—boy, that is such a great encouragement.

I hope that's what you take from this series: you can defeat the sin of anxiety through the power of Christ, not through your own power.

## Reading Matthew 6:25-34

Having given a long and rambling introduction, I want us to turn to Matthew 6:25:

> "Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink; nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? Which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature? So why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin; and yet I say to you that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Now if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not worry, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or 'What shall we drink?' or 'What shall we wear?' For after all these things the Gentiles seek. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about its own things. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." (Matthew 6:25-34)

## What is God's Love?

Before we talk about God's love, let's get some descriptions for what God's love is. What is God's love? Let me hear from you: God's love is holy. Okay, first one on the list. What's that? Unconditional. Eternal. Self-sacrificial. Okay. Perfect. Unchanging. Steadfast. These are great words. Sufficient. Covenantal. You guys got quite a few of them.

This is the list that Johnny Orteuvangelis, the author of the book that we're basing this study on, came up with:

- Holy
- Forgiving
- Satisfying
- Faithful
- Fatherly
- Everlasting
- Displayed in Christ
- Transforming

We're going to look at each one of those as they relate to us, as they relate to God, and as they relate to the sin of anxiety as we struggle with it.

## God's Love is Holy

When we talk about God's love, it is definitely a well-known topic, but it is maybe widely misunderstood. If we were to go out into the street today and ask people what God's love means, I think we might find that it means things like tolerance, overlooking things that are different than us, overlooking sin. Does it mean those things? Does it mean tolerance? Overlooking sin? Unconditional acceptance? Well, probably not, right? But given the lack of clarity around the topic, we do need to take a step back and consider all of these ways in which God's love works together.

First, we're going to talk about holiness. And holiness may seem like a weird place to start when we're talking about love. What does holiness have to do with love? I think in part this feels like a weird place to start because it's maybe easier for us to think of God through his individual attributes. God is holy. God's all-powerful. He's just. He's self-existent. And we can think about those as little pieces of a pie, and when we put them all together, that's what God is. But we have to reframe that a little bit, because God is not made up of parts. God is simple. He is all holy all the time. He's all just all the time. He's all wise all the time, all powerful all the time. It's not 20 percent love, 20 percent holiness, 20 percent justice.

So when we consider God's love, we have to consider God's love through the lens of all of God's other attributes. Holiness is a good place to start with that.

When we look at Scripture and how Scripture describes God unequivocally, we find that God is holy. God hates sin. I'm going to read a few verses:

> "Who is like You, O Lord, among the gods? Who is like You, glorious in holiness?" (Exodus 15:11)

> "O Lord, You have appointed them for judgment; O Rock, You have marked them for correction. You are of purer eyes than to behold evil, and cannot look on wickedness." (Habakkuk 1:12-13)

> "For You are not a God who takes pleasure in wickedness, nor shall evil dwell with You." (Psalm 5:4)

Because God is holy all the time, His love has to be consistent with that holiness. No evil thing can dwell with Him. No evil man comes to God as His father. And that's a big, big problem for us. It's certainly a big problem for me, because I know my own heart. I know the sin that's in my heart. I know my sinful actions.

So when we consider God's holiness, how do we get around that? I mean, this is really a truly insurmountable obstacle for us: our sin and God's holiness. These two things are not compatible.

Ephesians 2:4 gives us the answer. Paul has just finished describing our wicked hearts. He's described us as given up to the lusts of the flesh, consumed by sin, children of wrath just like the others. And then he has one of the greatest "buts" in the Bible. He says:

> "But God, who is rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses and sins, made us alive together with Christ (by grace you have been saved), and raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus." (Ephesians 2:4-5)

And Christ is the answer here. Christ's righteousness imputed to us moves us completely from the realm of God's righteous, holy, just wrath into His righteous, holy, just love.

We just simply cannot overstate how big of a deal this is. God, who is perfectly holy and who can tolerate no evil thing in His presence, freely forgives us of our sin. He imputes perfect justice and calls us righteous because of Christ—paying the punishment for our sin, taking our place. And the application of that righteousness to our hearts.

There's just simply nothing that we can do to replicate that on our own. In our natural state, we're dead in our trespasses and sins. Dead people don't do much except maybe decompose further, right? They're not doing anything to fix the situation that they're in. But something supernatural happens. Something outside of ourselves. That's the work of Christ applied to us.

Only once we realize how holy God is and how vile our sin is can we start to understand how big of a deal that is. We just cannot understand God's love until we understand His holiness.

## God's Love is Forgiving

We've already started to get to the second piece: God's forgiving love. Once we've considered God's love as a holy love, then we can consider God's love as a forgiving love. And it's really quite easy for us to misunderstand God's love as forgiving love.

When we talk about forgiving love, we talk about every single one of our sins being forgiven. Not 99 of our sins. Not all of our sins except for the really bad one that nobody knows about. Not all of our sins except for that thing that happened in high school that, if anybody knew about it, our life would be over.

If our sins are forgiven, if we have repented and trusted in Christ as our Savior, all of our sins are forgiven—not all of them except, but every single one of our sins. God knows that sin. He's forgiven you for that sin because of Christ's righteousness in His life, applied to us. Christ died on the cross for that particular sin that we don't want to give up.

How much of our anxiety, I wonder, is because we have sin that we don't believe that God could or has forgiven us for? And that's a question that we can only answer inside of our own hearts, inside of our own minds. But it's worth dwelling on: Is there sin that we think God cannot or has not forgiven us from? And if that's the case, if that's causing us anxiety, we need to consider the greatness of God's forgiving love. That sin has been forgiven.

And honestly, if we can contemplate the magnitude of the entirety of our sin—the worst things that we've done in our lives—being forgiven for us freely without some emotion, I think we're not fully gripping the magnitude of what has happened to us. Because that God, who did not spare His own Son but gave Him as a sacrifice for us, how will He not freely give us with Him all things?

God's forgiveness is a great cure for anxiety. We're at peace with God. In a very real sense, what else matters? Honestly, nothing else does. We're at peace with God. We're at peace with the Creator of the universe. We're at peace with the righteous Judge. And all else is secondary to that.

But there's maybe another way in which our anxiety relates to forgiveness. Maybe our anxiety stems from the fact that we have unconfessed sin in our life. When we talk about God's forgiveness applied to every sin in our life, that conditional forgiveness is absolutely still there. But if we're harboring unconfessed sin in our life, well, that is going to naturally create anxiety. It's going to create worry. It's going to create discord with God and a lack of fellowship, right?

So that just can't be the case: that we have unconfessed sin in our lives. We don't get "pet sins." We don't get that one thing that we want to hang on to and not confess but continue to do. And I think if we're honest with ourselves, some of our anxiety probably stems from unconfessed sin in our lives.

I can certainly think of times in my life where I thought, "I'll confess this sin once I've defeated it, once I've taken care of this sinful pattern in my life, then I can go to God and confess that." That's nothing more than pride in our lives. That's pride in our heart saying, "I can defeat this sin on my own." Rather, we should take that sin, confess it, turn from it. But we have to confess. We have to take that to God.

I'm going to turn to Psalm 32. No need to turn there with me, but I'm going to read about half the Psalm:

> "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit. When I kept silent, my bones grew old through my groaning all the day long. For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my vitality was turned into the drought of summer." (Psalm 32:1-4)

I think we can all recognize David's contemplation and meditation here. I think we can all recognize the weight that unconfessed sin has on our hearts. But David doesn't leave us there. He continues:

> "I acknowledge my sin to You, and my iniquity I have not hidden. I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the Lord,' and You forgave the iniquity of my sin. For this cause everyone who is godly shall pray to You in a time when You may be found; surely in a flood of great waters, they shall not come near him. You are my hiding place; You shall preserve me from trouble; You shall surround me with songs of deliverance. I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will guide you with My eye. Do not be like the horse or like the mule, which have no understanding, which must be harnessed with bit and bridle else they will not come near you. Many sorrows shall be to the wicked, but he who trusts in the Lord, mercy shall surround him. Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous; and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!" (Psalm 32:5-11)

In that Psalm, I think we can clearly see David's struggling with anxiety, with that physical weight that he feels in his bones—a drought of summer in his vitality. His energy is sucked away by this unconfessed sin. But as he confesses his sin and returns and is again in communion with God, he's rejoicing. He's leaping for joy. The Psalm ends with shouting for joy, all you upright in heart.

So we can see in that Psalm the very clear impact of confessing our sin and how that impacts our anxiety.

## God's Love is Satisfying

Next, I want to look at God's love as satisfying love. I think it's easy for many of us to intellectually affirm God's love as something that exists. But as we meditate on God's love, we need to realize that God's love is not a cold, hard intellectual fact. Rather, it's something that has a real impact on us every single day.

David tells us in Psalm 34 to taste and see that the Lord is good. He tells us in Psalm 63 that God's loving-kindness is better than life. And this is not just an intellectual "Oh, it is better than life." No, we're to taste and see that the Lord is good.

And that means really meditating on the ways that God's love has been manifested in your life. Fill your mind with scriptural truth about God's love. Fill your mind with verses from the Bible and great scriptural truths, to be sure. But you also need to fill your mind with concrete ways in which God has demonstrated His love to you in your actual life.

And as we fill our minds with the thoughts of God, our anxiety will flee. So that's my encouragement to you: this afternoon, tomorrow—meditate on the real ways in which God's love has been demonstrated to you in your life. And as we meditate on that more and more, our anxiety will not have room to be in our mind.

## God's Love is Faithful

God's love is a faithful love. God doesn't forget us. He doesn't change His mind. This truth is most encouraging in the midst of deep trials.

Are you deserted by your family? Are you betrayed by your friends? Your Father will never desert you. Your Savior will never betray you. Are you overcome by your sinful heart? Are you despairing of how God could love you? Your God knows all your sins—all the sins that you ever have committed, all the sins that you ever will commit. And yet He still loves you.

Nothing can separate us from the love of God. His compassion fails not. His mercies are new every morning.

I love my wife deeply, and I think she would tell you that. I think she would also tell you that there are probably many times that I have not acted lovingly to her. And as we examine all of our relationships, we love people, people love us, and they're going to sin against us. They're going to betray us. They will turn against us. They will desert us in our time of need. Despite that love, our heavenly Father will never do any of that. His love is everlasting. And that means that His love didn't have a beginning, and it won't have an end. He has loved you forever. He will love you forever. And that everlasting love should bring us great, great encouragement in the midst of trials. God has not forgotten you in your trial. God has not deserted you in your trial. Rather, He's with you in that trial. His love is with you, and it will sustain you.

## God's Love is Fatherly

Next, I want to consider God's love as a fatherly love. Psalm 103, verse 13 says:

> "As a father pities his children, so the Lord pities those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust." (Psalm 103:13)

Our earthly fathers may forget our weaknesses. We as earthly fathers may forget our children's weaknesses. More than once I've been told I expect too much from my five-year-olds, and it's probably true. But our heavenly Father never makes that mistake. He remembers our frame. He knows that we're dust. He pities us, or He has compassion on us. He does not forget who we are.

And we can be assured by the way that Christ does not forget who we are—because He was tempted in every way as we are. That's part of the beauty of Him taking on flesh: He understands our weaknesses.

God exercises perfect, tender fatherly love that puts to shame the love of even the best earthly father.

Isaiah chapter 49, verses 15 through 16, reminds us of the impossibility of a nursing mother forgetting her children. Mothers around the room, that's impossible, right? That you would forget your nursing child, that you would forget that they exist. But even if that crazy thing were to happen, God could never forget us. That's what that verse promises: even if in the crazy instance that a nursing mother forgot her children, our God will never forget us.

See, He tells us: "I have you inscribed on the palms of My hands." God, through adoption, makes us His children. And His love is not dependent on our merit. It's dependent on Christ's merit.

So when we worry, we're telling God that we don't believe that He loves us in the ways that He's promised that He has loved us or the way that He promises that He does love us. We're saying that we believe that God may have forgotten us. We're saying that maybe God loves us, but He can't protect us. But He can. He's all-powerful.

Jesus tells us in John chapter 15, verse 9: "Abide in My love." And abiding in God's love includes meditating on His love. And when we abide in His love, He goes on to tell us our joy will be full.

And this command to abide in Jesus's love does not happen in a vacuum. It happens right before—and you guys may not remember the next passage, but you will remember the content of the next passage. It happens right before Jesus tells His disciples, "They hated Me. They're going to hate you. They persecuted Me. They're going to persecute you." And that joining right there—the hating, the persecuting—is not separate from abiding in God's love. Abiding in Christ's love. And that's a great encouragement in our trials. We can abide in Christ's love. We're promised trials. We're promised persecution. But the command is given to us just before we're promised that: "Abide in My love, and your joy will be full."

## God's Love is Everlasting

Next, I want to consider God's love as everlasting. God doesn't change. We do. Beauty fades. Sharp minds become dull. And our lives are but a breath. But God's love is everlasting. He will never leave us. He will never forsake us. And that's just amazing.

## God's Love is Displayed in Christ

Next, I want to consider God's love displayed in Christ. We've danced around God's love displayed in Christ throughout the entirety of the lesson today. But God's love is not a distant, abstract thing. "God so loved us that He sent His only begotten Son to die for us." And Christ is the primary proof that we have of God's love manifested to us.

God did not withhold His own Son, but freely gave Him as a sacrifice for our sins. How can we worry when we truly contemplate that? That is the greatest gift that God could send us: His own Son to die for us. And if He was not willing to withhold even His own Son—His most precious Son—how can we doubt that His love will fail us in our daily trials, our daily sufferings, and our daily temptations?

## God's Love is Transforming

And lastly, I want to consider God's transforming love. As we come toward the end of the lesson, you may be sitting there thinking: "Well, thanks. You showed me all the different dimensions of God's love. But my life right now just does not feel like God's mercies are new every morning. I wake up every morning, and the mercies aren't new. The trials are new. And that can be a really, really discouraging place to be."

I hear you when you say that, because I've been there myself. And I feel the pain and the struggle of waking up every morning and saying, "I don't know where God's sustaining love is. I can't feel it in my life."

But to answer that question—that kind of question in our lives of how does that apply when we wake up every morning and the mercies don't seem new, the trials seem new, but the mercies seem like they're coming to the very end—I'm going to ask a throwback question to the series on the Beatitudes. So we're going to see how well the series on the Beatitudes stuck.

What is a blessing? A blessing is anything that brings us closer to Christ, anything that brings us closer to God.

God is in the business of transforming us and conforming us to the image of Christ. So when God promises that all things work together for good for those who are called according to His purpose, He means that. That good may not feel like good to us right here and right now. It may not be in accordance with what we think is best for our lives. But those whom God loves He disciplines. We're promised the refiner's fire. We're promised suffering. We're promised that as we go through that suffering, we're being conformed to the image of Christ.

And so God's transforming love means that the trials that we wake up to every morning are, by the transforming power of God's love, being used to conform us to the image of Christ. And that is the greatest good that could possibly happen to us.
